topic: Scope functions I: let, also & apply

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `let` returns whatever its lambda returns. The last expression is `it.length`, so `n` is the `Int` 5, not the original string.

questions.question: Inside this `apply` block, what does `color` refer to?
options: The `color` property of the new `Paint`, accessed through `this`
A `color` property of the enclosing View, because `apply` has no receiver
questions.explanation: `apply` runs the block with the object as its receiver (`this`), so unqualified `color` and `strokeWidth` resolve to the `Paint`'s own properties. `it` is not available in `apply`.

questions.question: Inside an `also { }` block, the receiver object is available as `this`, just like in `apply`.
questions.explanation: `also` passes the object as the lambda parameter `it` (which you can rename, e.g. `also { user -> }`). It is `apply` that makes the object `this`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `apply` always returns its receiver, so `list` is the mutable list after `add(2)`. The `Boolean` returned by `add` is ignored.

questions.question: In a ViewModel you want to log the filtered list in the middle of this chain without changing what flows into `map`. What should replace `???`?
questions.explanation: `also` returns the receiver unchanged and exposes it as `it`, which is exactly a side effect in the middle of a chain. The `let` version makes the chain the `Int` returned by `Log.d`, `apply` has no `it`, and `$this` inside `also` is the ViewModel, not the list.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: With `?.`, the `let` call is skipped entirely when the receiver is null and the whole expression is `null`. The lambda never runs, so `"Hi null"` is never built.

questions.question: In a ViewModel: `val saved = repository.newDraft().also { _draft.value = it }`. What is `saved`?
options: `Unit`, because the lambda ends with an assignment
It doesn't compile: assignments are not expressions
questions.explanation: `also` ignores whatever its lambda produces and returns the receiver, so `saved` is the draft. An assignment as the last statement of a lambda is fine, it just makes the lambda return `Unit`, which `also` throws away.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `b.also { ... }` evaluates to the old `b` (2) before the block runs, then the block sets `b = a` (1), then that saved 2 is assigned to `a`. Hence the classic swap idiom.

questions.question: When is `also` a better fit than `apply`? Select all that apply.
options: Inside an Activity, the block needs `this` to still mean the Activity
The block mostly passes the object as an argument to other functions, e.g. `cache.put(it)`
You want the block's last expression to be the result
The block mostly assigns the object's own properties
questions.explanation: `also` keeps the outer `this` untouched and names the object `it`, which reads well when the object is an argument. Assigning many properties reads better with `apply`'s implicit `this`, and neither function returns the block's result: that is `let`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The lambda's last expression is `println(...)`, which returns `Unit`, and `let` returns the lambda's result. So `r` is `Unit`, which prints as `kotlin.Unit`; returning the receiver is what `also` does.

questions.question: `user` is a mutable `var` property of a Fragment. Why does `user?.let { render(it) }` compile when `if (user != null) render(user)` does not?
options: `let` gets the value read once as a non-null `it`, unaffected by later changes
`?.let` locks the property so other threads can't modify it during the block
The compiler skips nullability checks inside inline lambdas
`let` copies the `User` object, so `it` is a defensive clone
questions.explanation: A mutable property can change between the null check and the use, so it can't be smart cast. `?.let` reads it once and passes that reference as a non-null `User` parameter. Nothing is locked or copied, `it` is the same object.

questions.question: For `val user: User? = repo.find(id)`, the type of `it` inside `user?.let { ... }` is the non-nullable `User`.
questions.explanation: `?.` only calls `let` when `user` is non-null, so `let` is invoked on a `User` and its parameter is typed `User`. That is why you can write `it.name` without `?.` inside.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Inside the inner `let`, `it` is 2, so it yields 20. The `+ it` sits outside the inner lambda, so it refers to the outer `it` (1), giving 21. Shadowing `it` compiles (the IDE only flags it), which is why naming nested parameters is recommended.

questions.question: `name` on `User` is a non-null `String`. What is the type of `names`?
questions.explanation: `body()?.let { ... }` is `List<String>?` (null when the body is null), and `?: emptyList()` removes the null case, so `names` is `List<String>`. Without the elvis it would stay nullable.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `apply` appends "x" and returns the same builder, `also` logs its length (1), and `let` appends "yz" to that same object and returns its length 3. All three operate on one `StringBuilder`, so `sb` is "xyz".

questions.question: `config?.apply { retries = 3 }` skips the block when `config` is null, and the whole expression evaluates to `null`.
questions.explanation: Safe-call works with any scope function: if `config` is null, `apply` is never called and the result is `null`; otherwise it configures and returns `config`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The elvis checks the result of the whole `user?.let { ... }` expression, not whether `user` was null. `log` returns `null`, so the `let` evaluates to null and the fallback runs too. Use `if (user != null) ... else ...` when both branches must be exclusive.

questions.question: What happens with this code in an Activity?
options: Compile error: inside `apply`, `this` is the `Intent`; use `this@MainActivity`
It works: `this` falls back to `MainActivity` because an `Intent` is not a `Context`
It works because `this` in a lambda always means the enclosing class
questions.explanation: In `apply`, bare `this` is always the innermost receiver, the `Intent`; Kotlin never picks a different receiver based on the expected type. `setClass(Context, Class)` therefore gets an `Intent` and fails to compile, and the fix is the labeled `this@MainActivity`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `Label` has no `title`, so inside `apply` the unqualified `title = "Profile"` silently resolves to the outer `Screen.title`. `text` exists on `Label` (innermost receiver wins), so the label gets the now-changed `Screen.title`. The outer object being modified by accident is the classic `apply` bug.

questions.question: In a Fragment factory, which of these give `args` a `Bundle` that contains the key `"id"`? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: `apply` and `also` return the bundle, and the last `let` explicitly returns `it`. The plain `let` returns what `putInt` returns (`Unit`), so `args` is `Unit`, and `apply` has no `it`, so that line doesn't compile.
